title: Replace Export / Backup / Import with structured Backup & Restore without credentials
description: Replace the four-mode export surface (configuration export, portable encrypted, same-machine backup, import) with a single structured Backup & Restore: one versioned plaintext JSON file containing saved non-secret settings overrides, SSH Connections and their groups — without credential records, secret IDs, or ContentDB content. Implements ADR-0015 (revises ADR-0011 §7), crash-safe journal protocol, exclusive configuration gate, and selectable merge/replace restore strategies.
acceptance_criteria: Backup creates a versioned 'nocx-backup' v1 JSON file (≤8 MiB) with non-secret settings overrides, all SSH connections (host/port/user/options without credentialId), and group tree (typed defaults subset without credential binding); credential records, secret IDs, SecretStore material, and content.db are absent. Restore accepts the file with selectable merge (default) or replace strategy. Merge preserves extra local connections/settings and direct credential binding only when host+effective-port are unchanged; group-level credential binding is always cleared. Replace makes connections and non-secret settings exactly match the snapshot. Both strategies preserve Credential metadata and keychain entries. Preview shows exact counts of included/changed/added/updated/removed/reset items and connections requiring credential reassignment, plus omission warnings. Restore requires a preview token that binds the exact file contents, strategy, and local state; a stale token forces re-preview and re-confirmation. Crash recovery via local journal (prepared → committed → idle): prepared rolls back, committed keeps state, unknown/corrupt journal returns recovery error. Configuration gate lock prevents concurrent backup/restore/profile/settings/open CRUD and fails closed with -32603 after unrecoverable journal state. New UI replaces the old Export / Backup / Import page: create backup button with counts/warnings, file picker with merge/replace radio and preview, confirm dialog, restore with token, success/failure handling, FileInput reset. ADR-0015 is created and ADR-0011 §7 is marked partially superseded. User documentation at docs/backup-and-restore.md covers the full workflow.
close_reason: Replaced the four-mode export surface with versioned structured Backup & Restore, ADR-0015, crash recovery, and user documentation

title: Encrypted private keys never use their stored passphrase: lookupKeyPassphrase has no caller
description:
internal/ssh/ssh_auth.go loadKey() parses the key and, on gossh.PassphraseMissingError, returns ErrEncryptedKey — it never calls lookupKeyPassphrase. So a passphrase stored via credentials.saveKeyPassphrase is written, referenced by PassphraseSecretID, threaded all the way into ConnectConfig, and then never read on the connect path. A passphrase-protected key cannot be used.

PRE-EXISTING, NOT A STORE-3 REGRESSION: verified against the baseline — origin/main's loadKey has the same shape and its lookupKeyPassphrase was equally uncalled. STORE-3 (nocx-r60) faithfully ported the dead path onto SecretID and flagged it in its report.

Two things are wrong at once: the feature does not work, and lookupKeyPassphrase is dead code called only from auth_chain_test.go:226, which AGENTS.md forbids. The fix is to wire it, not to delete it: on ErrEncryptedKey, resolve PassphraseSecretID through the SecretStore and retry with gossh.ParsePrivateKeyWithPassphrase, reading the plaintext inside Secret.Use so it never becomes a long-lived string.

## Acceptance Criteria
A key protected by a stored passphrase connects successfully. lookupKeyPassphrase has a non-test caller. The passphrase is read only inside Secret.Use and never returned as a string.

title: e2e enhanced-input on chromium is unstable: rapid submits race the tab-title assertion
description:
e2e/enhanced-input.spec.ts submits several commands in succession, each setting the tab title via OSC 0, and asserts the last one arrived. On chromium the membership of the failing set rotates between CI runs — :10, :38 and :61 have each failed and passed across four runs of this branch — and the failure signature for :61 varies too:

  run A: Expected 'MS-2', Received 'MS-1~00701~'   (BEL rendered literally, second sequence half-processed)
  run B: Expected 'MS-2', Received 'MS-0'          (never got past the first)

That is the shape of a race between the submit path and the 5s assertion window, not of a deterministic break. Supporting it: the webkit twin of :61 fails on main as well, so the test is fragile independent of this branch.

NOT PROVEN to be independent of this branch. main has been run once; a test that fails one run in three would very likely look green in a single sample. Settling it needs 2-3 runs on main, which was deliberately not spent — the branch's own auth regression (32 origin rejections per run, now fixed in e106b72) was the real signal hiding in these numbers, and it was found by reading the log rather than by counting failures.

If it is the product and not the test, the suspect is the submit path's handling of back-to-back OSC 0 sequences — the literal BEL in run A suggests a sequence being split across reads and not reassembled.

Next step when someone picks this up: run main 2-3 times to establish its own flake rate before touching code, then, if chromium is genuinely worse on the branch, bisect the frontend changes (the log.ts migration touched tabs.ts extensively, though not the submit path directly).

Related: nocx-bw2 (the suite's 13 inherited failures).

title: Orphaned secrets can still accumulate: the delete cascade is best-effort by design and has no janitor
description:
The credential delete cascade landed with nocx-7l4: credentials.delete now derives both secret keys, deletes metadata, then best-effort deletes the password and the key passphrase, aggregating errors so a failure is visible to the caller.

By design this can still strand a secret, and the design is correct: ADR-0011 §4 states that a brief unreachable orphan is safer than metadata pointing at a secret that is gone, so metadata goes first and secret deletion is best-effort. What the ADR assumes and we do not yet have is the other half — something that sweeps the orphans.

Two ways one appears:

1. Secret deletion fails after metadata is gone (keychain locked, transient error). The error surfaces to the caller, but nothing retries and the app can no longer name the secret.
2. The private key file at KeyPath is missing or unreadable when the credential is deleted. The passphrase is keyed by HashKey(keyBytes), so with the file gone the hash cannot be re-derived and the passphrase is unreachable forever. deriveKeyHashFromPath deliberately returns an error rather than skipping silently, so this is reported — but still not recoverable. Deleting a stale key file before its credential is an ordinary thing for a user to do, so this path is not exotic.

Needed: a janitor that can sweep by hash, and a decision about what it is allowed to delete — the keychain is shared with other applications, so 'delete anything we do not recognise' is not acceptable. That constraint is the reason this is not a five-line fix and why it was split out rather than folded into nocx-7l4.

Documented as a non-goal in .internal/reports/t6-delete-cascade.md; filed here so it is not lost with the report.

title: Four SSH options are editable, persisted and never applied: keepalive, readyTimeout, agentForward
description:
connections.ts offers keepaliveInterval, keepaliveCountMax, readyTimeout and agentForward. All four are collected in the form, sent through ProfileClient CRUD, stored by the profile store (profile.go), merged by mergeInto, and imported from Tabby configs (importer/tabby.go). Then they stop.

Verified by reference map — the four names appear in internal/profile/profile.go (12 hits), frontend/src/connections.ts (9), internal/importer/tabby.go (8), frontend/src/profiles.ts (4), and in NEITHER internal/ssh NOR internal/connection. connection.Resolver.buildConfig never copies them into ssh.ConnectConfig; ConnectConfig has no fields for them; ssh_dial.go hardcodes a 30s timeout; there is no keepalive ticker and no RequestAgentForward anywhere in the tree.

So a user sets a keepalive interval, it survives a restart, and the connection still dies on an idle NAT. Agent forwarding is offered and simply does not happen — which is the worst of the four, because someone may rely on it for a jump-host workflow and conclude the feature works.

This is a missing feature, not dead UI. Deliberately NOT fixed by deleting the controls (considered and rejected under nocx-1q2): the controls describe intended behaviour and the Tabby importer already populates them.

Fix: carry the four through Resolver.buildConfig into ConnectConfig, honour readyTimeout in ssh_dial.go instead of the hardcoded 30s, add a keepalive ticker driven by keepaliveInterval/keepaliveCountMax, and wire agentForward to RequestAgentForward. Until then, consider disabling the controls in the UI rather than leaving them silently inert.

Found while triaging nocx-1q2.

title: Hand-rolled PBKDF2 in the vault, justified by a dependency that already exists
description:
internal/credential/vault.go inlines its own PBKDF2 (RFC 2898, HMAC-SHA512) with the comment: 'We avoid the x/crypto/pbkdf2 dependency by inlining the core loop.'

The justification does not hold: golang.org/x/crypto v0.54.0 is already a direct dependency in go.mod — internal/ssh uses golang.org/x/crypto/ssh. Nothing is avoided by hand-rolling it.

Rolling a crypto primitive by hand is a standing risk even when the algorithm is simple: the vetted implementation gets constant-time review, test vectors and CVE tracking, and this one gets neither. It sits on the vault's key-derivation path, so a subtle error there weakens every secret stored on the non-keychain path.

Fix: replace with golang.org/x/crypto/pbkdf2 and delete the inlined loop. Verify against RFC 6070 test vectors before and after so the swap is provably behaviour-preserving — the derived key must be byte-identical or every existing vault becomes unreadable.

Predates PR11-T10 (nocx-1vr), which replaced the AES-CBC around it and deliberately left the KDF alone. Found during review of that work.

title: Only 3 of 9 e2e specs use the token-aware harness — the rest cannot authenticate on the headless devharness path
description:
e2e/harness.ts injects the Wails bindings (GetWSPort, GetWSToken) when NOCX_WS_PORT is set, which is what makes the headless devharness path work. Only auth.spec.ts, click-focus.spec.ts and command-editor.spec.ts import from './harness'. The other six — activity, activity-bell, clipboard, enhanced-input, seed, tabs, tab-title — import '@playwright/test' directly.

Under 'wails dev' that is harmless: the real bindings exist. On the devharness path window.go does not exist, GetWSPort() throws, main.ts falls back to port 9876 with an EMPTY token, and every connection is rejected with 'ws upgrade rejected reason=token'.

This is a trap, not just a limitation. Running one of those six headless produces a backend log full of token rejections, which reads exactly like a broken auth implementation. It cost the coordinator one false 'the positive path is broken' conclusion today; the token path is in fact fine (verified: zero rejections and 'session opened' when running a harness-aware spec).

Fix: switch the remaining six specs to import { test, expect } from './harness'. It is a no-op under wails dev by design, so CI behaviour does not change, and it makes the whole suite runnable headless — which is the cheap path that needs no display, no GTK and no EGL.

Discovered while verifying nocx-hl3.

title: e2e activity-bell clicks .tab-add while the alternate buffer hides it by design
description:
e2e/activity-bell.spec.ts:31 does page.locator('.tab-add').click() after entering the alternate buffer. The alt-screen design deliberately hides the tab strip — TabManager.syncAltScreenClass() puts .alt-screen on #app and the CSS sets '#app.alt-screen .tab-add { display: none }', so the terminal owns the full window and .tabbar stays above it only as a backdrop for the macOS traffic lights.

So the click can never land, and the test fails identically on main and on pr-11-boundary with 'element is not visible'. Confirmed by browser measurement: after the switch, .tab-add computes to display:none with a 0x0 box.

The test's intent is sound and worth keeping — a bell inside the alternate buffer must light the activity indicator, which is what tells you a background agent wants you back (nocx-5mf). Only its mechanism is wrong: it backgrounds the tab by clicking chrome the design hides.

Fix options: open the second tab BEFORE entering the alternate buffer and switch to it, or background the tab through a keyboard path that does not depend on hidden chrome. Do not delete the test.

Split out of nocx-bw2.

title: TABS-4: e2e coverage for both placements
description:
The existing suite asserts the horizontal bar (.tab-add, .tab). Those tests stay valid — horizontal is the default — and must keep passing. Add coverage for the vertical mode rather than replacing them.

Note for whoever picks this up: e2e currently runs only in CI, and only on non-draft PRs to main, so a placement regression would go unnoticed locally. See nocx-bw2.

title: STORE-6: ContentDB seam + stub (no SQLite dependency yet)
description:
ADR-0011 section 5. Declare the ContentDB capability and write the conversation and history repository interfaces against it. The SQLite implementation is NOT built here and no SQLite dependency enters go.mod — the seam carries a stub, exactly as config.Stub does today.

It becomes real with the first feature that needs it: nocx-de7 (output capture), nocx-dw3 (agent conversations) or nocx-4ff.6 (command history), whichever lands first. Conditions recorded for then: one database (content.db), not one per entity; WAL mode, because surviving a force-quit is the whole reason a desktop app takes a database; foreign_keys=ON; short transactions through one controlled write path.
acceptance_criteria: Repository interfaces exist and compile against a stub. go.mod gains no database dependency. The conditions for the real implementation are recorded where the implementer will find them.
close_reason:
STORE-6 landed: internal/content declares the ContentDB capability (Conversations/CommandHistory/Close) with two typed repositories and a logging Stub returning ErrNotImplemented — no generic Repository[T], no SQLite, go.mod and go.sum verified unchanged. The five conditions for the real implementation (one content.db, WAL, foreign_keys=ON, short transactions through one write path, and the 'removed from nocx' not 'securely erased' honesty constraint) are recorded in the package doc comment where the implementer will find them.

Took a revision pass: the first version shipped Save(ctx, id string) placeholders, which cannot carry a conversation and would have blocked nocx-de7 (P1) the moment it started. Now CommandRecord mirrors frontend/src/command-ledger.ts:12-25 — the shape nocx-de7 itself calls 'the right metadata and genuinely ready' — with pointers for the three fields that are nullable in TS, typed CommandStatus constants instead of a bare string, and no output field (ADR-0008 keeps output out of the ledger; capture is nocx-de7's job). Read methods included because a history repository that cannot list is useless to nocx-4ff.6's Ctrl-R browse. 11 tests.

title: EDITOR-W4: reconcile insertText with the focus-bounce
description:
Spec W4. Two redirect paths disagree: tabs.ts:441-442 (block selected) focuses AND inserts the character; tabs.ts:466 (focus drifted) only focuses and comments that it 'lets the key event propagate normally'.

DIAGNOSE BEFORE FIXING — the failure mode is not established. Focusing an element inside a bubbling keydown handler does not retarget the event already in flight, so the drift path plausibly LOSES the first character rather than doubling it; an earlier draft asserted double-insertion without evidence. Write the test and observe, on the textarea before W1 and on CM6 after.
acceptance_criteria: With a block selected, and again with focus drifted to <body>, typing one printable character puts exactly one character in the document — and the test exists for both engines so the migration cannot silently change the answer.

title: STORE-4: split ProfileStore by aggregate
description:
internal/profile/store.go:12-24 has one interface owning three aggregates — profiles, groups and credential metadata. Split into ProfileRepository, GroupRepository and CredentialMetadataRepository. No generic Repository[T]: query and consistency needs diverge, and a shared generic forces the widest contract on the narrowest store.

Also fix the lost-update bug: CRUD loads outside the mutex (store.go:108-120) while only save locks (:67-69), so two concurrent WebSocket requests can load the same snapshot and the later rename silently overwrites the earlier mutation.
acceptance_criteria: Three focused repositories behind their own interfaces. Concurrent updates to different records cannot lose one another; covered by a race test.
close_reason:
STORE-4 landed: ProfileStore split into ProfileRepository, GroupRepository and CredentialMetadataRepository, each behind its own interface; JSONStore still implements all three (one shared document) but every consumer now depends only on the narrow interface it uses — resolver, importer, transport and the composition root were all narrowed. No generic Repository[T].

The lost-update race is fixed and was proven first: the race test failed on the old code with 'profile id2 host = host2.example.com, want host2-modified.example.com (lost update!)'. Cause was CRUD loading outside the mutex while only save() locked it, so two concurrent WebSocket requests loaded the same snapshot and the later rename discarded the earlier mutation. The lock now wraps the whole load-modify-write cycle in all six mutating methods. Verified independently: go test -race ./... green across every package, and the locks stay inside internal/profile so no keychain call happens under a document lock (ADR-0011 §4).

title: EDITOR-W3: selection seam replaces the textarea getter
description:
Spec W3. Remove the textarea getter; add onSelectionEnd(cb) which fires with the selected text when a selection gesture completes and copies nothing itself. Rewrite tabs.ts:480-491 to register a callback applying the existing shouldCopy policy and the clipboard write.

The DOM mechanics of 'a selection finished' belong inside the editor; the policy of 'should this be copied' belongs outside it. Define the event boundary explicitly — mouse, keyboard, double/triple click, collapse — and return a disposable so listeners do not survive tab closure (Tab.close() at tabs.ts:708).
acceptance_criteria: Selecting text in the editor copies under the same shouldCopy rules as today. No consumer reaches into the editor's DOM. The subscription is disposable and disposed on tab close.

title: PR11-T11: hygiene — committed .orig artifact, gofumpt, whitespace, dead UI fields
description:
Evidence the commit gate never ran on the branch: frontend/src/tabs.ts.orig is a committed 44 KB conflict artifact (AGENTS.md: no dead code, delete it); gofumpt -l flags internal/profile/profile.go; git diff --check reports extensive trailing whitespace starting at frontend/src/connections.ts:71.

Also dead UI: keepalive interval, ready-timeout and agent-forwarding are editable at connections.ts:488-542 but reach no ConnectConfig field — the UI silently promises liveness and security behaviour that is not implemented. Either wire them or remove the controls. Credential.KeyPath is never carried through credential resolution (connections.ts:273-289).
acceptance_criteria: tabs.ts.orig deleted. gofumpt -l clean. git diff --check clean. Every editable SSH option either reaches the connection or is removed from the UI.
close_reason:
Nothing left to do — every item was already resolved, verified independently rather than taken on report.

- frontend/src/tabs.ts.orig: deleted in e5ad9f2 (the 44 KB merge artefact).
- gofumpt: 'gofumpt -l .' now flags only internal/credential/secret.go and secret_test.go, which are in flight under nocx-l7o and belong to that worker.
- trailing whitespace: 'git diff --check origin/main...HEAD' is clean. connections.ts was rewritten in fc37a6a (innerHTML -> createElement/textContent for the XSS fix), which took the whitespace with it.

The dead-UI item was investigated and deliberately NOT actioned as written. keepaliveInterval, keepaliveCountMax, readyTimeout and agentForward are not dead UI: they are collected, sent, persisted and populated by the Tabby importer, and then never reach ssh.ConnectConfig. That is a missing feature, and deleting the controls would have destroyed the description of intended behaviour. Split out as nocx-49x with the full reference map.

title: PR11-T9: make dial and resize cancellation-safe
description:
Second plan. Cancellation currently stops at the initial TCP dial: direct and jump handshakes call blocking gossh.NewClientConn (ssh_dial.go:59, :154) without closing the socket on ctx.Done(), and jump-target dialing uses non-context-aware jumpClient.Dial (:86). ClientConfig.Timeout does not wrap manually performed handshakes.

Also ssh_channel.go: closeCb runs outside closeOnce (:33-38) so repeated or concurrent closes repeat the underlying close, and Resize discards its context (:46-54) and can block after disconnect — which violates AD-7's uniform channel/disconnect contract.
acceptance_criteria: Cancelling the context during any handshake phase closes the socket and returns promptly. Repeated and concurrent Close is idempotent. Resize honours its context and does not block after disconnect. Covered by race tests.
close_reason: Landed in 82e4555. Handshakes run under a watchdog on ctx.Done() that closes the net.Conn to unblock gossh.NewClientConn (no context form in v0.54.0); the result channel is buffered so the goroutine cannot leak, and the caller sees ctx.Err() rather than 'use of closed network connection'. Jump-target hop uses DialContext. Pool waiters on an in-flight dial can cancel without inheriting a half-built connection — T8's deferred item. Resize honours its context and does not block after disconnect; closeOnce from 9d411ec verified by test rather than assumed. Acquire gained a ctx parameter and kept defaultDial as the loud-failing placeholder. Nine tests, each shown to fail without its fix, with the mutation lists in the report.

title: Warn before a paste that would self-execute — only in RAW, never in ALT_SCREEN or RUNNING_RAW
description:
Complement to nocx-hi2. That bead makes composed text safe in enhanced mode: a paste lands
in the DOM editor and cannot execute until an explicit submit. This bead covers the case
where the editor is not in play.

Tabby warns on every multi-line paste because it has no editor and cannot know what is on
the other end — which is why the owner finds it exhausting. We have the input-ownership
state machine (frontend/src/input-state.ts), so the rule can be sharp:

  PROMPT_READY  — no warning. Paste lands in the editor, visible and editable. The
                  common case, and it stays silent.
  ALT_SCREEN    — no warning. In vim/less a multi-line paste inserts lines; nothing
                  executes. Warning here is exactly the nagging we are avoiding.
  RUNNING_RAW   — no warning. A program is reading stdin; multi-line input to a REPL
                  or cat is ordinary.
  RAW           — WARN. Unintegrated shell at its own prompt: our editor is not
                  involved, the text goes to readline, and a newline is accept-line.
                  This is the only state where a paste executes without review.

Trigger is not "the text has multiple lines" — it is "the text contains a newline that
will be taken as accept-line". A single trailing newline qualifies.

The dialog must be fail-safe: cancel sends NOTHING. A partial send would be worse than no
warning at all, because it executes a prefix the user never reviewed.

Payoff worth noting: this is the state machine earning its keep. Without it we would be
back to Tabby's position — warn always, or never.

Depends on nocx-hi2 being resolved first: while the hand-rolled wrappers leak, enhanced
mode is not actually safe, and warning only in RAW would give a false sense of coverage.
notes:
CORRECTION (2026-07-25): this is ALREADY MOSTLY IMPLEMENTED. I described an existing feature as new design without reading the code first.

frontend/src/tabs.ts:632-642 already does:
  - editor visible -> insertText, no confirm ('The editor is a composer — a multi-line paste is expected and needs no confirm')
  - text.includes('\n') && _bufferType === 'normal' -> window.confirm('Paste multi-line text?')
  - alternate screen -> no confirm
The comment there even says 'This is Tabby's exact condition.'
Covered by tabs.test.ts:737 and :770.

So the trigger is already the newline (not 'multi-line-ness'), and PROMPT_READY and ALT_SCREEN are already correct.

WHAT ACTUALLY REMAINS — much smaller than this bead originally claimed:
1. The gate keys on _bufferType === 'normal', not on the input-ownership state. So a paste into a RUNNING program in the normal buffer (cat, a REPL, ssh asking for a password) still prompts, when it should not — that program is reading stdin and a multi-line paste is ordinary. Narrow the condition to the RAW state from input-state.ts instead of the buffer type.
2. window.confirm is a blocking browser modal — precisely the ergonomics the owner dislikes in Tabby. Replace with a non-blocking in-app affordance.

Rescoped accordingly. Still depends on nocx-hi2: while the hand-rolled wrappers leak, enhanced mode is not actually safe, so 'no confirm at the prompt' rests on a promise the submit path does not yet keep.

title: [bug] TerminalRenderer advertises capabilities wterm silently does not have
description:
renderers/types.ts declares one flat TerminalRenderer interface, and WtermRenderer
implements the parts it cannot support as silent no-ops rather than as absent
capabilities: setReadOnly (wterm.ts:114, "@wterm/dom has no disableStdin"), and per the
codex review also alt-buffer reporting, OSC 7, OSC 133, selection, OSC 52 and bracketed
paste (wterm.ts:68, :75, :103 — verify each before acting).

Consequence for input ownership: tabs.ts:380-394 makes the terminal read-only when the
editor takes the prompt. Under wterm that call does nothing, so the only thing keeping
keystrokes out of the terminal is focus. The enhanced prompt is therefore not safe on
wterm, and nothing says so — the renderer reports success.

AD-8 asks for interfaces that make modules trivially replaceable; an interface a
substitute can only satisfy by lying is the opposite. Options: split into capability
interfaces the renderer can honestly decline, have the composition root refuse enhanced
mode on a renderer lacking the capability, or drop wterm from enhanced mode outright.

Related: nocx-id3 (wterm wheel handling), ADR-0001 (wterm kept switchable for re-testing).

title: [epic] Agent mode: drive the pi/omp loop over RPC, render it in our own surface
description:
Own the AI experience end to end: our editor is the input, our blocks are the output,
and the agent loop runs headless underneath. NOT agent-as-TUI.

CONFIRMED PROGRAMMATIC SURFACE (pi docs + locally installed pi 0.80.10):
  SDK               embed in Node.js — not our path, we are Go
  RPC mode          stdin/stdout JSONL  <-- our path
  JSON event stream print mode with structured events
  TUI components    for building extension UI — explicitly not wanted here
Sessions: --session-id / --session / --fork / --resume, tree-structured.
Models: --provider / --model / --api-key — bring-your-own, incl. fully local, which
is vision.md:75 (Phase 3) verbatim.

WHY THIS SHAPE: a TUI agent puts the session in ALT_SCREEN, where the input-ownership
machine hands the whole viewport to the app and the DOM editor disappears by design.
Driving the loop over RPC keeps us out of ALT_SCREEN entirely, so the editor keeps
input ownership and we render the dialog — the point of AgentInputTarget in ADR-0004
section 3.

AGENT IS A FAMILY, NOT A PRODUCT (AD-8): pi and omp (omp.sh) share the
PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR env contract and the same extension API, and both emit milestone
agent_end events mid-work — evidence: /home/dev/repos/orca src/shared/pi-agent-kind.ts,
which treats them as one kind. So we build against the CONTRACT and both become
implementations behind one interface; which agent runs is configuration, not code.
Caveat: that compatibility claim comes from Orca's source, not from omp's own docs
(omp.sh returns 403 to fetch and omp is not installed here). Verify before relying.

FRAMING NOTE: pi speaks JSONL over stdio; our control plane is JSON-RPC 2.0 over WS
text frames (AD-1). Different framing, same dialect — the agent module adapts at its
own boundary rather than leaking JSONL upward.

WORK, ROUGHLY:
- Go module behind an interface: spawn the agent child, speak JSONL, map its event
  stream to our control plane, handle cancellation and process lifecycle
- AgentInputTarget on the editor: separate draft and history from the shell target,
  explicit mode switch, never a magic prefix (ADR-0004 section 3)
- rendering: prompt -> response is structurally command -> output, so agent turns are
  blocks in the DOM scrollback and reuse the ledger and block model — no separate
  chat pane
- context from current work: feed the ledger (cwd, host, exit codes, durations) and
  block output into the agent's context; map a tab to a durable --session-id
- decorations per target: agent mode renders prose plus mentions of blocks and files,
  which is why the decoration set belongs to the ACTIVE TARGET, not to the editor
  (see nocx-2gf)
- secrets: block output can carry credentials. What leaves the machine for a remote
  model needs an explicit rule (relates nocx-23v). Local models make this moot; BYO
  remote ones do not.

FIRST STEP BEFORE DESIGN: read docs/rpc.md from the pi package for the real wire shape.
DEPENDS ON: nocx-2gf (editor core) — there is no agent surface without it.

title: [epic] External backends: multi-backend frontend seam, then the remote relay
description:
Let the frontend talk to MORE THAN ONE backend — the embedded local one plus remote
ones reached over a relay — and let a remote session survive a dropped connection.
Two phases, and phase A is the one that must not be deferred.

TODAY: frontend/src/ipc.ts WSClient holds a single `this.ws` to one host:port
(ipc.ts:267) and SessionHandle hangs off it. There is exactly one backend, implicitly.
"Which backend" is not a concept anywhere in the frontend.

PHASE A — THE SEAM (do this while it is still cheap):
- a Backend abstraction above WSClient: connect / open / send / onData / close, with
  the Wails-embedded local backend as implementation #1. Per AD-8 this is manual
  constructor injection at the single composition root, and per AD-8's own words the
  same seam is the plugin seam.
- session identity becomes (backendId, sessionId), not sessionId alone. AD-7 keeps
  session-id server-authoritative — but "the server" becomes "that backend", so the id
  is only unique within its backend. Retrofitting this after tabs, restore, ledger and
  blocks all key on a bare sessionId is a wide, unpleasant change; adding it now is
  mechanical.
- a tab is bound to a backend endpoint, and the semantic-layer resolver from the
  semantic epic binds to the SESSION, so it automatically follows.
Phase A ships value on its own: it is the refactor that stops every later feature from
silently assuming "the backend is on this machine".

PHASE B — THE RELAY: a remote process holding the PTY so a session survives a network
drop, plus port forwarding. Reference implementation to study, already on this
machine: /home/dev/repos/orca — src/relay/ is 148 files with a framed binary protocol
and a version-negotiating handshake (EXIT_CODE_VERSION_MISMATCH = 42 lets the client
distinguish incompatible from transient and skip reconnect backoff), delivered by
src/main/ssh/sftp-upload.ts, with "remote PTY lease" semantics.
Our architecture already reserved the room:
  - AD-2: one Go codebase, multiple build targets, remote helper named explicitly
  - AD-1: the version byte AND a reserved `metadata` msg-type were allocated up front
    so this feed ships without a wire break
  - AD-9: the bounded per-session output ring with offset acks IS lease/replay
    semantics — phase B extends it across a host boundary rather than inventing it
Honest price: shipping and updating a binary per arch/libc, protocol versioning on
both sides, lifecycle and cleanup, and the "why is your process running on prod"
conversation. This is why it is phase B and why warpify (nocx-pu4) comes first —
warpify needs none of it.

OBSERVABILITY (required, and the reason it lands here): the moment there are two hops
a log line without correlation is useless. Needs:
- a correlation/trace id per session that travels frontend -> backend -> relay, carried
  through Go via context per the existing log/slog contract
- a real frontend logging interface behind an abstraction (AD-8). Today there are ~19
  ad-hoc console.* calls across 5 files and no seam; architecture.md:204 still lists
  frontend log forwarding as an unconfirmed ASSUMPTION — this epic confirms it and
  specifies transport and verbosity.
- HARD CONSTRAINT from vision.md:97 — no telemetry, ever. Observability here means
  local structured logs the user can read and forward on purpose. Nothing phones home.

title: [epic] Semantic command line: in-band highlighting, validation, completion, ghost-text
description:
Make the input surface understand the command being typed: syntax colouring, semantic
colouring (alias / function / not-found), argument validation, ghost-text suggestions
and a completion popup. Absorbs nocx-4ff.6, nocx-4ff.22, nocx-4ff.23.

THE BINDING RULE — EVERYTHING IS IN-BAND. A session can be local, SSH, SSH through a
jump host, or forwarded; the number of hops is unbounded. Any mechanism that asks the
Go backend a question ("does this path exist", "is this on PATH") answers about the
machine nocx runs on, NOT the machine the session lives on, and breaks at the first
hop. Concretely: standing in /etc/nginx on prod, a local stat() on nginx.conf succeeds
because the path also exists on the laptop — the highlight then lies at exactly the
moment the cost of being wrong is highest. Silently-wrong semantics are worse than
absent semantics.

So the shell at the far end answers about itself, in the byte stream, the same way
OSC 133 already works. This keeps AD-6 intact (the backend never sniffs bytes; the
frontend parses OSC) and costs zero transport-specific code — the same mechanism
serves local, SSH and jump identically. It is also why this epic depends on warpify:
without integration on the far host there is nothing to answer.

WHERE THE FACTS COME FROM:
- prompt-time snapshot: nocx.zsh:37-40 already prints D, A and OSC 7 back to back in
  precmd. A fourth printf carries aliases + functions (with a change counter so the
  same payload is not resent every prompt). This gives alias/function-aware colouring
  that a sidecar process CANNOT provide, because interactively-defined aliases exist
  only in the live session.
- resolution queries (is this on PATH, does this path exist) answered by the session's
  own shell — behind an interface bound to the SESSION, never a global backend call.
  No resolver for a transport => the semantic layer degrades to plain tokenisation.
- ranking from the command-ledger: cwd + host + exit code + duration are already
  recorded, so suggestions can prefer what SUCCEEDED here rather than what is merely
  frequent. This is a genuine edge over Warp's spec-catalogue ranking.

COMPLETION, AND WHY IT BEATS WARP: bridge to the user's own bash-completion / zsh
compsys instead of curating Fig-style specs. 100% coverage of what is actually
installed — internal tools, make targets, package.json scripts, kubectl plugins — with
zero spec maintenance. Warp cannot match this structurally; their model is spec-first.
Risk: invoking zsh compsys headlessly is materially harder than bash compgen, so bash
and zsh are separate beads and bash goes first. Completion scripts execute code —
state it in the ADR rather than implying it.

FAIL-SOFT INVARIANT (mirrors fail-open): shell syntax is hostile — quoting, $( ),
heredocs. When the tokenizer is unsure it renders plain text and NEVER renders red,
and validation NEVER blocks submit. A false alarm costs more than a missing highlight.

SECRETS: ghost-text must not resurface a password typed inline. The ledger marks such
records and suggestions skip them (relates to nocx-23v).

DEPENDS ON: editor core (nothing to draw with) and warpify (nothing to ask on a
remote host).
notes:
DEPENDENCY CORRECTED (2026-07-25): warpify (nocx-pu4) no longer BLOCKS this epic — that was too coarse and it froze local work behind remote work.

Warpify is required for semantics to work on a REMOTE host at any depth. Locally the shell is already integrated, so tokenising, colouring, history and completion all work without it. Blocking the whole epic on warpify meant no syntax highlighting on a laptop until a bootstrap works on production servers.

Now a relates_to. The remote half of this epic still depends on nocx-pu4; say so per-task when those tasks are written, not at the epic level.

title: Long-output blocks truncate: xterm scrollback is capped at 10k lines before freeze
description:
Found in the nocx-4ff.18 audit (open question Q2 in spike/dom-scrollback/DESIGN-NOTES.md).

A DOM block is serialized from the xterm buffer between the C and D markers, at D. The xterm Terminal is constructed with scrollback: 10000 (frontend/src/renderers/xterm.ts:138), so a command emitting more than ~10k lines has already lost its earliest output by the time we serialize — the frozen block silently starts mid-output, with nothing telling the user it was cut.

Before the DOM scrollback this was benign (the terminal simply scrolled), which is why it was never a bug. Now it is lossy: the block is the permanent record.

Options: temporarily raise scrollback while a command runs and lower it after freeze; stream-serialize incrementally as lines scroll out instead of once at D; or accept a cap and render an explicit 'output truncated, N lines dropped' marker at the top of the block.
acceptance_criteria:
• A command emitting well over the scrollback cap either keeps its full output in the block, or the block visibly states that output was truncated — no silent loss.
• The chosen strategy does not regress the freeze-time perf budget measured in the spike (<100ms for 5k lines).
• Covered by a vitest case over the serializer with a synthetic over-cap buffer.

title: ADR-0008: command blocks as a keyboard-first ledger, not cards
description: ADR-0008: command blocks in nocx are a KEYBOARD-FIRST LEDGER OF TRUSTED COMMAND LANDMARKS over one continuous xterm (WebGL canvas), NOT Warp-style cards. Per-command record: app-owned command text, cwd, host, start/end xterm IMarkers (never cached line numbers), timestamps, status (running/success/failure/interrupted/unknown), exit code, trust. Output bytes NOT retained by default (secrets). 5 pillars: (1) IDE-symbol-list navigation incl prev/next FAILURE + command palette/filters; (2) safe 'Edit and run again' (app-owned command into editor, warn on cwd/host drift), never rerun scraped text; (3) attention/failure queue (bg-tab notify, next-unresolved-failure, slow threshold, session summary); (4) durable LOCAL provenance (search across sessions, pin/bookmark), no cloud; (5) output actions via byte-interval/snapshot capture LATER, not canvas scraping. First increment (=nocx-4ff.5): gutter glyph on command row + prev/next + prev/next-failure keyboard nav (jump scrolls xterm, return-to-live) + lightweight inspector (command/cwd/host/status/exit/duration/copy/edit-and-run-again). Deferred: sticky headers, hover toolbars, collapse, output copy, share, click-anywhere block select. Divergences from Warp: no card-per-command, no green success confetti (neutral landmarks; color only for running/failure/focus), no sticky header, no collapse-until-authoritative-output, no share-as-default. Gutter is a sibling div, pointer-events:none, IMarker-anchored, rAF-coalesced, alt-screen hides chrome, marker.onDispose cleanup, fail-open. Direction pressure-tested with Codex 2026-07-24.

title: ADR-0006: marker-only prompt mode (enhanced-input shell contract)
description: Marker-only prompt mode (enhanced-input shell contract). Two static-at-spawn contracts: NOCX_SHELL_INTEGRATION=1 (markers+visible prompt, safe baseline) vs NOCX_PROMPT_MODE=marker-only (suppress prompt + DOM editor owns input), plus NOCX_SESSION_ID. Suppression is a PER-PROMPT overlay reapplied at the LAST prompt hook (frameworks like p10k/oh-my-zsh/starship rewrite PS1 every precmd and would clobber a one-time assignment AND the B marker); zsh suppressor last in precmd_functions, bash reordered so PS1=marker-only is the final action. NOT save/restore of a PS1 string (stale) — overlay model; restore = remove hooks, let framework regenerate. DOM keyboard ownership requires A->B, not A alone (missing B => keys raw). Secondary prompts PS2/PS3/read stay native. Fail-open needs coordination beyond the flag: spawn enhanced PTY only after frontend readiness; a state-independent native-mode escape that RESTORES a visible prompt (one-shot control op, not per-prompt signaling). Nested/remote: MVP top-level only via NOCX_SESSION_ID; remote negotiated explicitly. Decided after Codex review; refines ADR-0004 s2 save/restore mechanism.

title: Keyboard navigation over command blocks (prev/next command, prev/next failure)
description:

• Part 1 (command-record model) — DONE. frontend/src/command-ledger.ts is built and wired: opened on submit with command/cwd/host/marker, closed on the D marker (tabs.ts:285,310,348).
• Part 2 (gutter glyphs) — DROPPED by owner decision, commit cf0ac45 'remove gutter/decorations — user confirmed they look terrible'. The DOM scrollback replaced the landmark idea outright: each command is now a visible block with its own status header, so a gutter has nothing left to mark. Dead code to delete: frontend/src/gutter.ts, gutter.test.ts, spikes/gutter-spike.ts — none are imported by tabs.ts. The renderer's registerMarker()/IMarker API stays; the scrollback uses it.
• Part 4 (inspector) — SUPERSEDED. Command, cwd, duration, status and exit code are on every block header; copy actions are in the ⋮ menu; edit-and-rerun moved to nocx-4ff.20.

What remains is part 3, keyboard navigation, which nothing has replaced.

## Acceptance Criteria

• Shortcuts move the selection to the previous/next command block and to the previous/next FAILED block, scrolling it into view in .scrollback-area (selection model already exists: BlockManager._selectedBlockId, single-select, Escape deselects).
• A 'return to live output' control scrolls back to the live xterm region and clears block selection.
• Navigation is inert during alt-screen (mode === 'fullscreen') and when the editor owns a keystroke that should be text.
• Deleting frontend/src/gutter.ts + gutter.test.ts + spikes/gutter-spike.ts is part of this bead.
• Covered by vitest; shortcuts documented wherever keybindings land (see nocx-8yg.7).

title: Linux distribution: AppImage release build in CI + support envelope
description:
Deferred deliberately, not forgotten. Design: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-22-distribution-and-updates-design.md (D1).

A Wails Linux build is dynamically linked against GTK, WebKitGTK, libsoup and glibc, so an artefact built on Ubuntu 24.04 runs on the distributions that happen to match and nowhere else; a tarball installs no dependencies, and a .desktop file inside it integrates with nothing. Shipping it would mean choosing and testing a support envelope for a platform with no identified user today.

Reopen when BOTH exist: a person who will actually run it, and a decision about which distributions are supported. At that point the realistic choice is AppImage (linuxdeploy plus its GTK plugin, which brings its own class of WebKitGTK-versus-host breakage) rather than a bare tarball. Note this also moves docs/architecture.md:179, which currently says Windows/Linux are Phase 3 and is accurate while this is deferred.
notes: In scope per ADR-0006 (D1 reversed): maintainer runs nocx on Linux. Scope = AppImage build in CI (linuxdeploy + GTK plugin), linux/amd64 artefact + linux manifest entry, stated support envelope (glibc floor, bundled WebKitGTK). Parallels nocx-a75.1 for macOS; blocks the linux Platform impl and the updater's linux half.
close_reason: AppImage build-linux job + manifest linux entry + README support envelope (glibc 2.35, bundled GTK/WebKitGTK) landed. YAML valid, action/toolchain parity with the proven macOS job, --version smoke check confirmed against main.go. E2E is CI-only (next tag). Committed.

title: Frontend readiness signal: a tab reports whether it actually started
description:
TabManager's constructor calls newTab() without awaiting it (frontend/src/tabs.ts:443), and Tab.start() catches its own failure and renders a .pane-error notice into the pane (frontend/src/tabs.ts:356). So a constructed TabManager is fully compatible with a terminal that never started — there is currently no way for anything to ask 'did the terminal actually come up?'.

Work: Tab exposes whether its renderer mounted and its PTY session opened; TabManager exposes a promise resolving when the initial tab reaches that state. The existing swallow-and-show-a-notice behaviour stays for the UI — it simply stops counting as success.

Useful on its own (it is the honest startup signal the app lacks), and a hard prerequisite for the updater's health check: without it the updater would bless a release whose terminal failed to start, then delete the rollback copy. Found by adversarial review of the distribution design, docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-22-distribution-and-updates-design.md (S7.5).
acceptance_criteria: A test proves the promise resolves for a genuinely started tab and does not resolve for one whose start() threw.
close_reason: Tab.ready + TabManager.initialTabReady landed; resolves on genuine start, rejects on failure, .pane-error UI preserved. 46 vitest green + tsc clean. Committed.

title: Payload round trip and manifest verification, proven before anything swaps a bundle
description:
The two mechanisms the whole updater rests on, landed and proven while a failure is still harmless. Design: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-22-distribution-and-updates-design.md (S9).

1. Payload round trip: a genuinely built .app through ditto -c -k then ditto -x -k, asserting the executable bit, symlink targets, lipo -archs still showing both slices, codesign --verify --deep --strict still passing (Wails applies an ad-hoc signature and packaging must not damage it), and that the extracted bundle launches. This is a macOS integration test, not a unit test with a fixture. The first design draft planned to extract with Go's archive/zip, which restores nothing on its own and would have produced regular non-executable files with no symlinks — this test is what makes that class of error impossible to ship.

2. Manifest verification against the ed25519 keyring: valid, tampered body, key outside the keyring, valid signature from a second key in the keyring, malformed base64. Fixture keys generated in the test, no network.
acceptance_criteria: Both tests pass against a real CI-produced artefact, and the round trip fails if the archive is created with plain zip instead of ditto.
notes: Rescoped per ADR-0006: payload round-trip is now per-platform behind the Platform seam — macOS .app (ditto/codesign/lipo, as designed) PLUS a lighter Linux AppImage round-trip (exec bit + integrity survive download then replace; no bundle tree or symlinks). Manifest verification (ed25519 keyring) is cross-platform and runs on the Linux dev box and in macOS CI.
close_reason: Manifest verify acceptance matrix (5 cases) + linux structural round-trip pass locally; darwin .app round-trip + archive/zip negative test are darwin+NOCX_INTEGRATION CI-gated and compile under GOOS=darwin. Negative test made deterministic (coordinator fix). Committed.

title: Go tests flake under load: session Done channel and ws size contract time out
description:
Two Go tests fail intermittently and pass in isolation, both by timing out rather than by asserting anything false:
- internal/session TestRealRegistry_DoneChannel — 'Done channel never closed' after 5.10s
- internal/transport TestWSServer_SizeContract_OpenAtSize — 'read: i/o timeout' after 5.00s

Caught by the pre-commit hook on a commit that changed only .beads/*.jsonl — no Go code at all — and the same tests had passed on the preceding commit minutes earlier. Re-run individually: both ok. Full 'go test -race ./...' afterwards: all green. So the failure is load-dependent, not a regression.

Both use fixed deadlines around real goroutine and socket work, which is the same class as the e2e flake in nocx-epm: a duration that holds on an idle machine and loses when the box is busy. -race makes it worse by slowing everything it instruments.

Worth fixing rather than tolerating — a hook that fails for unrelated reasons trains people to re-run until green, and the next real failure gets re-run too. Look at whether the deadlines can be replaced by waiting on the actual signal, and whether these two can stop competing for the machine with the rest of the suite.
acceptance_criteria: go test -race ./... passes twenty consecutive runs on a loaded machine, and neither test uses a fixed deadline as its synchronisation.

title: Auto-update mechanism
description:
Keep an installed nocx current without a manual re-download. Design: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-22-distribution-and-updates-design.md (S7).

The design survived three adversarial review rounds; round 3 broke an earlier phase-machine design in five places and it was replaced rather than patched. The load-bearing idea: THE FILESYSTEM IS THE TRUTH, THE JOURNAL RECORDS INTENT. The record holds device+inode of the old and new bundles; reconciliation observes which identity sits at which path and derives state from that. There is no prepared/swapped/healthy phase to go stale between a mutation and the write describing it. Versions cannot do this job (a same-version re-release, a reinstall and a downgrade share version strings), and string path comparison cannot either (symlinks and the /Applications vs /System/Volumes/Data/Applications alias).

Work: internal/update with Check/Apply/Reconcile/ReportHealthy; ed25519 keyring verification of the manifest; archive preflight via archive/zip BEFORE invoking ditto; extraction via /usr/bin/ditto -x -k --noqtn (archive/zip cannot restore a bundle); atomic exchange via unix.RenameatxNp with RENAME_SWAP; advisory flock on an open descriptor (never O_EXCL, which survives SIGKILL); bounded try-lock at startup so the terminal never waits on someone else's download; auto-rollback after three launches that reach Go without confirming health; legible refusals; UI notice and README.

Depends on the payload round-trip proof and the frontend readiness signal — both are prerequisites, not part of this bead.
acceptance_criteria: A running nocx detects a newer published release and can move the user to it, and the update it installs launches.
notes: Rescoped per ADR-0006: cross-platform. Platform-agnostic core (manifest fetch+verify, semver, download, crash-consistency transaction: journal/flock/reconcile/health/auto-rollback) + the Platform seam (see the Platform seam bead) with darwin (section 7) and linux (AppImage) impls. Stay on Wails v2; v3 built-in updater rejected.
close_reason: Auto-update transaction core + Platform seam orchestration + Wails wiring + UI notice + README rollback landed. Check/Apply/Reconcile/ReportHealthy with device+inode journal, flock, auto-rollback; ReportHealthy gated on initialTabReady. Coordinator review caught+fixed a Linux Apply self-copy bug, a flock-unlink race, and added Apply e2e tests. Full gate green (build, linux+darwin vet, all tests). Real GitHub fetch + darwin hardware exchange are CI/manual. Committed.

title: macOS code signing and notarization for distributable builds
description:
An unsigned .app downloaded from the internet is refused by Gatekeeper — the user gets 'damaged and cannot be opened', not a warning they can click through. Every route to another person's Mac needs this, and an updater needs it twice over: it replaces the running application, and an unsigned replacement will not launch.

Needs an Apple Developer account (paid, annual), a Developer ID Application certificate exported into CI secrets, codesign with hardened runtime, and notarytool submission plus stapling. Wails supports signing in wails.json but the notarization step is ours to script.

Cost and ownership are the owner's call, not a technical detail to assume: this is the first item in the project that requires a paid account and long-lived secrets in the repository.

Linux has no equivalent gate; AppImage and .deb run unsigned. This bead is macOS-only by nature.
acceptance_criteria: A CI-produced macOS build downloaded on another Mac opens without a Gatekeeper refusal.
close_reason: Out of scope per D3 of docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-22-distribution-and-updates-design.md. There is no Apple Developer ID and there will not be one, so this cannot be done: notarization requires Developer ID, which requires paid enrolment; no third-party service signs in its own name (SignPath stores YOUR certificate, it does not issue one); and Homebrew closed the workaround — --no-quarantine is removed from brew and from 2026-09-01 every cask must pass Gatekeeper. An earlier design kept a dormant 'sign if secrets exist' branch in the pipeline; review round 1 correctly called it speculative and a half-truth, since real Developer ID distribution needs signing order, hardened runtime, entitlements, notarytool and stapling rather than a secrets toggle. What IS in scope and stays: Wails' unconditional ad-hoc signature, which packaging must preserve and verify. Reopen only if a team ID ever becomes available.

title: Release builds for macOS in CI
description:
Produce an installable macOS artefact from CI and publish it. Design: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-22-distribution-and-updates-design.md (S4, S5, S6).

SCOPE CORRECTION (2026-07-23, after three review rounds): macOS only. Linux is deferred (D1) because a Wails Linux build is dynamically linked against GTK/WebKitGTK/libsoup/glibc, so an Ubuntu-built artefact is not a portable 'linux amd64' artefact, and there is no identified Linux user. docs/architecture.md:179 therefore stays as written and is NOT amended.

Work:
- internal/version with Version/Commit/Date set via -ldflags (Wails v2.13 passes them to both universal slices).
- Patch wails.json info.productVersion from the tag: the object does not exist today, so 1.0.0 is Wails' default and the plist would otherwise disagree with the linked Go version. Releases restricted to stable vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH because CFBundleVersion has a narrower grammar than semver.
- ci.yml gains workflow_call and LOSES its push tags trigger (otherwise every release runs the suite twice).
- release.yml on tags, calls ci.yml so a release cannot exist without green backend/frontend/e2e on that commit. workflow_dispatch is dry-run only: a manual run has no tag and cannot produce the release URLs the manifest asserts.
- Build on macos-15 (explicit image), verify with lipo -archs and codesign --verify --deep --strict, package .dmg via hdiutil and .zip via ditto -c -k --keepParent --noqtn.
- Publish job (separate, so the signing key never sits in a job running build tooling) generates manifest.json, signs it with ed25519, attaches both to the release.

Ends with a downloadable build installed BY HAND on another Mac. No updater code here.
acceptance_criteria: A tagged commit produces downloadable macOS and Linux artefacts from CI, and each one launches on a clean machine of its platform.
close_reason: macOS release CI shipped in da73bab (merged); blockers nocx-hj1/nocx-vu9 now closed. Linux artefact moved to nocx-mbu (done). Closing.

title: [epic] Epic: Distribution and updates
description:
Getting nocx onto other people's machines and keeping it current. Design (three adversarial review rounds): docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-22-distribution-and-updates-design.md

The two doc decisions this epic said had to be revisited before work started are now RESOLVED:
- docs/architecture.md:179 ('MVP is macOS-only; Windows/Linux are Phase 3') — STAYS AS WRITTEN. Linux is deferred (nocx-mbu): a Wails Linux build is dynamically linked against GTK/WebKitGTK/libsoup/glibc, so an Ubuntu-built artefact is not portable, and there is no Linux user today.
- docs/vision.md:89 ('no app-store or packaged distribution') — IS AMENDED, inside nocx-a75.1/nocx-a75.3, to describe GitHub Releases, unsigned builds, a self-hosted update chain, and the manual quarantine step.

The constraint that shaped everything: there is no Apple Developer ID and there will not be one. Signing and notarization are therefore out of scope (nocx-a75.2, closed), the first install needs a manual xattr, and update integrity is ours — an ed25519-signed manifest verified against a compiled-in keyring. Homebrew is not an escape: --no-quarantine is gone from brew and every cask must pass Gatekeeper from 2026-09-01.

Order matters and is deliberate: an updater defect can remove the application itself, so the artefact path ships and gets used by hand (a75.1) and its two load-bearing mechanisms are proven (nocx-3dk) before anything replaces a bundle automatically (a75.3).
close_reason: Distribution & updates epic complete. Cross-platform auto-updater shipped: Platform seam (darwin+linux), ed25519 manifest core, crash-consistency transaction (journal-by-inode, flock, auto-rollback), Wails wiring + UI notice, AppImage CI build + support envelope, frontend readiness gating. All 8 children closed; make ci green (gofumpt/golangci-lint/go test -race/build/frontend); GOOS=darwin vet clean. Real GitHub fetch + darwin hardware exchange validate on the next tagged CI release. Not pushed (awaiting maintainer).

title: Settings registry: declare user-facing settings in one place so the settings screen is generated, not remembered
description:
Problem this solves is process, not code: deferred settings get forgotten. The terminal clipboard work left two user decisions living as ad-hoc state — the OSC 52 write grant (ClipboardGate) and copy-on-select (shouldCopy, currently unconditional) — with nothing but a bead to remind anyone to surface them when the settings screen arrives. This backlog has already demonstrated that reminders drift: three items finished in code sat open in the tracker and were offered as next work.

Invert it. Declare each user-facing setting once — id, label, description, default, current value, and whether it persists — and have the settings screen RENDER THAT LIST rather than being hand-written. Then surfacing a setting is not something to remember; forgetting requires deleting an entry, which is a deliberate act rather than an omission.

Not speculative: five consumers are already filed — nocx-8yg.5 (font family/size), nocx-8yg.6 (colour schemes), nocx-8yg.7 (keybindings), plus the two clipboard decisions above. All four settings-facing beads are blocked by this one, so none of them can be picked up without going through the registry.

Frontend-only and buildable now; it does not wait on storage. nocx-jap (persistent config) then binds the registry to a backing store, and entries flip from ephemeral to persisted in one place. Name matches the domain language already in use — internal/config and 'settings', not a third word for the same thing.
acceptance_criteria: Every user-facing preference is declared in one module; ClipboardGate and copy-on-select read their values from it; adding a preference requires no edit to a settings screen.
close_reason:
Delivered by STORE-5 (nocx-9m5) in the ADR-0011 epic. internal/settings declares each setting once — key, section, label, description, default, validation, data class and control kind — and frontend/src/settings.ts RENDERS that list: it switches on decl.control and groups by decl.section, with no literal setting key anywhere in the screen. Adding a setting is one MustRegister* call and no frontend change, which is exactly the inversion this bead asked for: forgetting now requires deleting a declaration, a deliberate act.

Scope note, so this is not read as more than it is: the MECHANISM is delivered, not the full catalogue. Only clipboard.osc52Suppressed is declared today. The consumer beads this one blocked — nocx-8yg.5 (font family/size), nocx-8yg.6 (colour schemes), nocx-8yg.7 (keybindings) and the copy-on-select toggle — are now unblocked and each adds its own declaration.

It also turned out not to be frontend-only as the description assumed: the registry is Go, because a secret-class setting must be backed by SecretStore and must have no read path (ADR-0011 §2).

title: e2e activity-bell is flaky under parallel load (fixed sleeps race the shell)
description:
e2e/activity-bell.spec.ts fails intermittently when the whole suite runs, and passes 5/5 when run alone. Observed on webkit: 'expect(locator).toBeAttached() failed' on the activity indicator. Pre-existing — the spec landed in ffb36b7, an ancestor of 1537d18, and the terminal-clipboard work did not touch it. Surfaced incidentally while verifying that change.

Cause is time-based synchronisation. The test types a command that enters the alternate screen, sleeps 5s in the SHELL, rings the bell, then sleeps 30s. It then waits a fixed 2000ms before backgrounding the tab and a fixed 6000ms before asserting. Five spec files share one wails dev instance across parallel workers, so under load the shell can take long enough to start that the bell lands after the 6s window closes and the assertion runs before the indicator lights.

Fix the same way e2e/clipboard.spec.ts was fixed: replace fixed sleeps with state-based synchronisation — wait for an observable signal that the shell has actually reached each stage rather than guessing at durations. Do NOT raise the timeouts; that hides the race and it returns on a slower machine or in CI.

CROSS-REFERENCE (2026-07-26): nocx-9ci covers the same test with a different and evidenced diagnosis, and the two should be reconciled before either is worked.

nocx-9ci: the test does page.locator('.tab-add').click() after entering the alternate buffer, and the alt-screen design deliberately hides the tab strip — TabManager.syncAltScreenClass() puts .alt-screen on #app and the CSS sets '#app.alt-screen .tab-add { display: none }'. Confirmed by browser measurement: after the switch, .tab-add computes to display:none with a 0x0 box, and the element at the click point is the tabbar acting as the traffic-light backdrop. So the click can never land, in isolation or under load.

That makes 'flaky under parallel load' an incomplete description of at least part of this. It does not necessarily make it wrong — the webkit toBeAttached failure recorded here is a different assertion from the click timeout, and fixed sleeps racing the shell could still be a real second effect on top. Do not merge the two beads blindly; establish first whether the toBeAttached failure survives once the click is fixed.

Note the branch also restored a missing piece that changed this test's behaviour: 557e87d had dropped the tab.onBufferChange subscription, so #app never gained the alt-screen class at all and the terminal covered the bar without it being hidden. Restored in d463fa1 (merged f42368a). Any flakiness measured before that commit was measured against a different bug.
acceptance_criteria: The full suite passes ten consecutive runs, and the spec contains no fixed sleep used as synchronisation.

title: Persistent config: internal/config is an in-memory stub, so no user decision survives a restart
description:
internal/config/config.go is a 47-line Stub: a map in memory, with Load() and Save() as logged no-ops. Nothing a user chooses is remembered across restarts.

This became load-bearing with the OSC 52 clipboard gate: writes are denied by default and the banner offers 'Allow clipboard writes', but with no storage that grant lasts only until the app is closed, and 'Don't show again' cannot mean what it says. The same gap blocks every other setting the terminal will want — font, theme, keybindings, copy-on-select toggle.

Needs a real implementation behind the existing Config interface (Load/Save/Get/Set), a file location that fits macOS conventions, and a bound method so the frontend can read and write settings. Keep it behind the interface per AD-8; the Stub stays as the test double.
acceptance_criteria: A user decision written through Config survives an app restart, and the OSC 52 grant plus 'Don't show again' both persist.
notes:
Half done, and deliberately not closed. The storage half landed with the ADR-0011 epic (nocx-6ek): internal/config's in-memory Stub is DELETED and replaced by internal/settings, a typed registry persisted through storage.DocumentStore in the OS config dir, served over seven JSON-RPC methods and rendered by a generated settings screen. A decision written through the registry does survive a restart.

But this bead's acceptance names two things, and the second is unmet: 'the OSC 52 grant plus Don't show again both persist'. frontend/src/clipboard.ts:174 still holds that decision as a private _suppressed field. The setting clipboard.osc52Suppressed is declared and served — the clipboard gate simply never calls it. See the note on nocx-3cc for the exact remaining hop. Close this when the gate reads and writes the setting.

title: OSC 52 grant: bind the user's decision to the program, not the whole app
description:
Today an OSC 52 clipboard-write grant is all-or-nothing for the app (Warp's model). Least privilege says the grant should name the program: allowing Claude Code to write the clipboard is far narrower than allowing anything running in any tab.

Identity MUST come from the kernel, never from anything the program controls. The obvious cheap route — matching the terminal title — is worthless: the title is set by the program itself (OSC 0/2), so a hostile program writes 'Claude Code' and inherits the grant. Use the PTY's foreground process group (TIOCGPGRP on the pty fd) and resolve it to an executable path. internal/pty/pty_local.go already holds cmd *exec.Cmd, so the fd and the child are in reach. Match on the full path, not the basename — 'claude' can be any file on PATH.

Where this degrades, and it is exactly where the risk is highest: over SSH there is no local process for the remote program, so the foreground process is 'ssh' and the grant collapses to 'any host you connect to'. Same inside tmux, where it collapses to 'tmux'. The SSH case likely needs a grant keyed by host rather than by process — decide that when SSH lands (nocx-9le).

Needs: a foreground-process lookup in the backend, a control-plane message to carry the identity to the frontend (AD-1/AD-6), and per-program grant state in the frontend policy. Depends on persistent config (the grant must outlive a restart to be worth having).
acceptance_criteria: A clipboard-write grant applies to one program identified from the kernel, not to the whole application, and a differently-named program does not inherit it.
notes:
The persistence half is now half-built and stops one call short. internal/settings declares clipboard.osc52Suppressed (a toggle, publicConfig) and it is served over the wire by settings.describe / getAll / set, persisting through DocumentStore. But frontend/src/clipboard.ts:174 still keeps the decision as a private _suppressed field, so 'Don't show again' in banner.ts still dies with the process.

Remaining work is small and specific: have the clipboard gate read clipboard.osc52Suppressed at startup and write it through settings.set when the user picks 'Don't show again', instead of setting _suppressed. Landed 2026-07-26 with the ADR-0011 epic (nocx-6ek); the settings worker was told to escalate rather than change the frontend, which is why the last hop is unbuilt rather than forgotten.

title: Wire ValidateCwd into the OSC 7 path once SSH lands
description: internal/shellintegration.ValidateCwd is implemented and unit-tested but deliberately not called: nocx-5mn.2 parses OSC 7 in the frontend per AD-6 and uses the path directly. Every session today is local, so the host arrives empty and validating it would cost an IPC round trip per cd to confirm an empty string. AD-5 assigns the backend ownership of local-vs-remote and host validation, and that ownership only starts paying when the host comes from a remote shell. Decision taken with the repo owner, recorded in the interface doc comment so the code is not deleted as dead by a future reader.
acceptance_criteria: The OSC 7 handler routes host+path through ValidateCwd, a hostile or unexpected host is rejected rather than displayed, and a test covers the remote case.

title: shellintegration.ParseCwd contradicts AD-6 (backend must not parse OSC)
description: internal/shellintegration/shellintegration.go declares ParseCwd(data []byte) and ParsePromptMarker(data []byte) — a backend parser fed raw terminal bytes — and internal/app/app.go constructs it into the composition root. AD-6 is explicit that the VT frontend parses OSC 7/133 via parser.registerOscHandler and that 'the backend does not sniff the byte stream'; the conditional dependency was DISCHARGED by ADR-0001 with 'the backend never parses OSC'. AD-5 still leaves the backend a real job — it owns local-vs-remote and validates the host, while 'the frontend only supplies the desired path' — so the interface should take a path, not a byte stream. Nothing calls ParseCwd today, so this is drift in the shape of the seam rather than a live violation, but implementing nocx-5mn.2 against the current signature would cement it.
acceptance_criteria: The shell-integration seam takes a frontend-supplied path and returns validated {host,path}; no backend API accepts raw terminal bytes; AD-6 and the code agree.
close_reason:
Interface reshaped to AD-6: ValidateCwd(host, path) replaces ParseCwd(data []byte), so no backend API takes raw terminal bytes; ParsePromptMarker went with it rather than being kept speculatively. internal/app now holds the interface instead of the concrete Stub, matching the repo's interface-first/DI rule. Covered by internal/shellintegration tests.
Deliberately NOT wired into the OSC 7 path — decided with the repo owner and recorded both in the interface doc comment and in nocx-3p1. Every session is local today, so the host arrives empty and validating it would buy an IPC round trip per cd to confirm an empty string. The comment says plainly that it is unwired by choice, so it is not deleted as dead code.

title: [bug] Tab title disappears while the mouse is over the tab
description: Hovering a tab hides its title entirely. The rule is frontend/src/style.css '.tab:hover .tab-title', which applies a two-layer -webkit-mask-image intended only to fade the title under the 22px close button. The two layers combine to mask the whole label instead. Note WKWebView is the target engine, so verify the fix in the real app, not only in Chromium.
acceptance_criteria: Hovering a tab leaves the title readable, with at most a fade where the close button overlaps it.
close_reason: Verified by the repo owner in the real WKWebView app: the title stays at full strength and fades only under the close button. Fixed by dropping -webkit-mask entirely in favour of an absolutely-positioned ::after gradient overlay (34px, right edge, fading to the tab's current background via a --tab-bg custom property, z-index 1 under the close button's 2). Masks had failed twice here — first two layers compositing unpredictably, then a single gradient dimming the whole label — because WKWebView's defaults for mask-size/mask-repeat diverge from Chromium's. An ordinary positioned gradient has no engine-dependent behaviour.

title: [bug] New tab flashes 'Terminal' before showing the directory
description: Opening a tab shows 'Terminal' for a moment, then it becomes the directory name. Cause is visible in frontend/src/tabs.ts: _defaultTitle is initialised to FALLBACK_TITLE ('Terminal', line 17/51) and written into the DOM in the constructor (line 87), while the real name only arrives after 'await this.client.openSession(...)' resolves (lines 183-188). The tab is therefore painted with a placeholder every time.
acceptance_criteria: A newly opened tab never displays 'Terminal'; it shows the directory from its first painted frame.
close_reason: The constructor no longer paints FALLBACK_TITLE into the DOM; the label stays empty until openSession resolves with the directory name. Guarded by e2e/tab-title.spec.ts, which snapshots the label via a MutationObserver at the instant the tab node is inserted — before the fix that snapshot read 'Terminal'. Passes in both Playwright engines.

title: Closing a tab with a running program asks for confirmation
description: Closing a tab kills its session immediately. Other terminals ask first when something is still running, because closing a tab in the middle of a Claude Code session or a build loses work. Needs a way to tell 'a program is running' from 'an idle shell' — the foreground process differing from the shell, or OSC 133 command markers (nocx-5mn) — and a confirmation that is skippable for an idle shell so the common case stays one click.
design:
How Tabby does it (tabby-local/src/components/terminalTab.component.ts, canClose): it asks the PTY for the shell's child processes and, if there are any, shows '"{command}" is still running. Close?' with Kill / Cancel. No shell integration, no OSC 133 — just the process tree.

We can be more precise than a child list. The PTY exposes the terminal's FOREGROUND PROCESS GROUP via tcgetpgrp(fd): when it differs from the shell's own pid, a command is running in the foreground right now. That is exactly the moment to catch, and it is better than enumerating children because a backgrounded job ('sleep 100 &') is a child but must not block closing, while tcgetpgrp correctly ignores it. It also names the command: look up the pgid to report 'claude is still running'.

Placement: the backend owns the PTY, so this is a session query, not something the frontend can compute — and it must not be inferred from the byte stream (AD-6). Add a control-plane request, e.g. a JSON-RPC 'busy' method taking a sessionId and answering {busy, command}. The frontend asks before closing and only prompts when busy, so an idle shell still closes in one click.

Note the answer is a snapshot and can go stale between the query and the confirmation — that is acceptable here; the cost of a rare wrong prompt is far below the cost of losing a running session.
acceptance_criteria: Closing a tab running a program asks first; closing an idle shell does not.

title: New tab is named Terminal; name it after the working directory
description: Every comparable terminal labels a tab with its folder rather than a generic word — Warp shows '..cuments/repos/meshynet'. Our fallback is the literal 'Terminal', which tells the user nothing and makes several tabs indistinguishable until a program sets a title. Use the session's working directory as the fallback, shortened from the left when it does not fit, and keep letting OSC 0/2 override it while a program is running. OSC 7 already carries cwd changes (nocx-5mn.2) — the two should share one source of truth rather than each inventing a title.
acceptance_criteria: A new tab shows its working directory instead of 'Terminal', a program's title still wins while it runs, and the directory returns when that program exits.
close_reason: Closed

title: Right-click in the terminal opens the webview context menu (Reload / Inspect Element)
description: Right-clicking anywhere in the app shows WebKit's own menu with Reload and Inspect Element — developer surface leaking into a shipped terminal. Wails exposes EnableDefaultContextMenu in the app options; it should be off outside development. Right-click is also wanted later for paste (nocx-8yg.4), so whatever suppresses the default menu must leave that path open.
acceptance_criteria: Right-click in the terminal does not show Reload / Inspect Element in a non-dev build.
notes:
NOT fixed — reconfirmed by the owner with screenshots. EnableDefaultContextMenu:false is set (main.go:38) but is necessary, not sufficient, for two reasons found in the wails v2.13.0 source:
1. internal/frontend/desktop/darwin/window.go:62 — defaultContextMenuEnabled := bool2Cint(debug || frontendOptions.EnableDefaultContextMenu). In dev the native menu is ALWAYS on, so 'Reload / Inspect Element' under wails dev says nothing about the shipped build.
2. internal/frontend/runtime/desktop/contextmenu.js — with the default '--default-contextmenu: auto' the native menu still shows when the target is an input/textarea, contentEditable, or text is selected. xterm keeps focus in a helper textarea, so the Cut/Copy/Paste/Spelling menu reproduces in a production build too.
Fix therefore needs '--default-contextmenu: hide' (inherited, like --wails-draggable) plus our own menu. The owner wants the menu to be ours, which overlaps nocx-8yg.4 (copy-on-select + right-click paste).
close_reason: Right-click no longer raises the WebKit menu. EnableDefaultContextMenu:false was necessary but not sufficient, as the bead's own notes recorded: the fix is --default-contextmenu:hide on the pane, inherited like --wails-draggable. Right-click now pastes instead. Note the comment in style.css was corrected during review — a later listener cannot un-cancel an already-cancelled default, so the CSS is defence in depth rather than the mechanism the original note assumed.

title: Hovering a tab hides its label
description: The mask-image gradient copied from Tabby's tabHeader.component.scss fades the title under the action buttons on hover. Tabby sizes it for its own button cluster (mask-size: calc(100% - 80px) auto, 80px auto); with our single close button the 80px fade swallows most of a 200px tab, so the label disappears instead of fading under a button. Size the mask to the buttons we actually render, or drop the mask and let text-overflow: ellipsis do the work.
